ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Overview
Management also measures the results of comparable store and club sales, or comparable sales, a metric that indicates the performance of our existing stores and clubs by measuring the change in sales for such stores and clubs, for a particular period from the corresponding prior year period. Walmart's definition of comparable sales includes sales from stores and clubs open for the previous 12 months, including remodels, relocations, expansions and conversions, as well as eCommerce sales. We measure the eCommerce sales impact by including all sales initiated digitally, including omni-channel transactions which are fulfilled through our stores and clubs as well as certain other business offerings that are part of our ecosystem, such as our advertising net sales. Sales at a store that has changed in format are excluded from comparable sales when the conversion of that store is accompanied by a relocation or expansion that results in a change in the store's retail square feet of more than 5%. Sales related to divested businesses are excluded from comparable sales, and sales related to acquisitions are excluded until such acquisitions have been owned for 12 months. Comparable sales are also referred to as "same-store" sales by others within the retail industry.

question: How did the primary drivers for iPhone and Wearables, Home and Accessories net sales change for Apple Inc. between fiscal year 2020 and fiscal year 2025?
ground_truth_answer: In fiscal year 2020, iPhone net sales decreased primarily due to the absence of new iPhone models in the fourth quarter and foreign currency weakness, while Wearables, Home and Accessories net sales increased due to higher sales of AirPods and Apple Watch. By fiscal year 2025, iPhone net sales increased due to higher net sales of Pro models, whereas Wearables, Home and Accessories net sales decreased primarily due to lower net sales of Accessories and Wearables.

answer:
In fiscal 2020, iPhone net sales decreased compared to 2019 primarily due to the absence of new iPhone models in the fourth quarter of 2020 and the weakness in foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar, partially offset by the introduction of iPhone SE in the third quarter of 2020. [AAPL FY2020, Item 7, AAPL_FY2020_2020-09-26:114]

In fiscal 2025, iPhone net sales increased compared to 2024 due to higher net sales of Pro models. [AAPL FY2025, Item 7, AAPL_FY2025_2025-09-27:136]

This means the primary iPhone driver changed from timing and currency-related headwinds in 2020, with some support from iPhone SE, to product-mix strength from higher Pro model sales in 2025. [AAPL FY2020, Item 7, AAPL_FY2020_2020-09-26:114] [AAPL FY2025, Item 7, AAPL_FY2025_2025-09-27:136]

Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data > Note 2 – Revenue Recognition
The Company has identified up to three performance obligations regularly included in arrangements involving the sale of iPhone, Mac, iPad and certain other products. The first performance obligation, which represents the substantial portion of the allocated sales price, is the hardware and bundled software delivered at the time of sale. The second performance obligation is the right to receive certain product-related bundled services, which include iCloud, Siri and Maps. The third performance obligation is the right to receive, on a when-and-if-available basis, future unspecified software upgrades relating to the software bundled with each device. The Company allocates revenue and any related discounts to these performance obligations based on their relative SSPs. Because the Company lacks observable prices for the undelivered performance obligations, the allocation of revenue is based on the Company’s estimated SSPs. Revenue allocated to the delivered hardware and bundled software is recognized when control has transferred to the customer, which generally occurs when the product is shipped. Revenue allocated to the product-related bundled services and unspecified software upgrade rights is deferred and recognized on a straight-line basis over the estimated period they are expected to be provided. question: How did Meta Platforms' accounting policy for recognizing credit losses on available-for-sale debt securities change between its fiscal year 2019 and fiscal year 2023 10-K filings?
ground_truth_answer: In its fiscal year 2019 10-K, Meta indicated that unrealized losses were charged against interest and other income, net, only when a decline in fair value was determined to be other-than-temporary, and noted that no such impairment charges had been recorded. In its fiscal year 2023 10-K, the policy evolved to align with newer accounting standards, where allowance for credit losses on AFS debt securities are recognized as a charge in interest and other income (expense), net, based on an assessment of expected credit losses, with any remaining unrealized losses included in accumulated other comprehensive income.

question: How did Tesla's explanation for why recognizing its unrecognized tax benefits would not affect its effective tax rate evolve between fiscal year 2016 and fiscal year 2022, and what specific tax examinations are highlighted in the 2022 filing that were not mentioned in 2016?
ground_truth_answer: In both fiscal years 2016 and 2022, Tesla explained that recognizing its unrecognized tax benefits would not affect its effective tax rate because the resulting tax benefits would increase a deferred tax asset that is fully offset by a valuation allowance. However, the 2022 filing specifically notes that the company is currently under examination by the IRS for the years 2015 to 2018, whereas the 2016 filing did not mention any current IRS examinations, only that tax years 2003 to 2015 remained subject to examination.
target_sections: ITEM 8. FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND SUPPLEMENTARY DATA
answer:
In fiscal year 2016, Tesla said that unrecognized tax benefits of $198.3 million, if recognized, would not affect its effective tax rate because the tax benefits would increase a deferred tax asset that was currently fully offset with a full valuation allowance. [TSLA FY2016, Item 8, TSLA_FY2016_2016-12-31:553]

In fiscal year 2022, Tesla gave the same basic explanation, stating that unrecognized tax benefits of $572 million, if recognized, would not affect its effective tax rate because the tax benefits would increase a deferred tax asset that was currently fully offset by a valuation allowance. [TSLA FY2022, Item 8, TSLA_FY2022_2022-12-31:467]

So, the explanation did not materially change between 2016 and 2022; it remained that recognition would increase a deferred tax asset that was fully offset by a valuation allowance, although the 2022 filing used the phrasing “fully offset by a valuation allowance” rather than “fully offset with a full valuation allowance.” [TSLA FY2016, Item 8, TSLA_FY2016_2016-12-31:553] [TSLA FY2022, Item 8, TSLA_FY2022_2022-12-31:467]

The 2022 filing specifically highlighted that Tesla was currently under examination by the Internal Revenue Service for the years 2015 to 2018. [TSLA FY2022, Item 8, TSLA_FY2022_2022-12-31:467]

It also stated that additional tax years within the periods 2004 to 2014 and 2019 to 2021 remained subject to examination for federal income tax purposes. [TSLA FY2022, Item 8, TSLA_FY2022_2022-12-31:467]

By contrast, the 2016 filing said only that tax years 2003 to 2015 remained subject to examination for federal purposes, tax years 2003 to 2015 remained subject to examination for California purposes, and tax years 2007 to 2015 remained open for examination in other U.S. state and foreign jurisdictions, without mentioning a current IRS examination for 2015 to 2018. [TSLA FY2016, Item 8, TSLA_FY2016_2016-12-31:553]

question: Based on the 2016 and 2021 10-K filings for Meta Platforms, how did the company's accounting policy description regarding the measurement period for business combinations change between these two fiscal years, and what specific valuation estimates were highlighted in the 2016 filing that were omitted from the 2021 description?
ground_truth_answer: The 2016 filing described the measurement period as 'one year from the acquisition date' and explicitly listed significant valuation estimates such as future expected cash flows from acquired users, acquired technology, and trade names, along with useful lives and discount rates. In contrast, the 2021 filing updated the policy to state the measurement period is 'not to exceed one year from the acquisition date' and omitted the specific list of valuation estimate types, focusing instead on the general allocation of fair value to tangible assets, liabilities, and intangible assets.

Item 8.Financial Statements and Supplementary Data > Business Combinations
We allocate the fair value of purchase consideration to the tangible assets acquired, liabilities assumed and intangible assets acquired based on their estimated fair values. The excess of the fair value of purchase consideration over the fair values of these identifiable assets and liabilities is recorded as goodwill to reporting units based on the expected benefit from the business combination. Allocation of purchase consideration to identifiable assets and liabilities affects the amortization expense, as acquired finite-lived intangible assets are amortized over the useful life, whereas any indefinite-lived intangible assets, including goodwill, are not amortized. During the measurement period, which is not to exceed one year from the acquisition date, we record adjustments to the assets acquired and liabilities assumed, with the corresponding offset to goodwill. Upon the conclusion of the measurement period, any subsequent adjustments are recorded to earnings. Acquisition-related expenses are recognized separately from business combinations and are expensed as incurred.

In October 2021, the FASB issued ASU No. 2021-08, Business Combinations (Topic 805): Accounting for Contract Assets and Contract Liabilities from Contracts with Customers (ASU 2021-08), which clarifies that an acquirer of a business should recognize and measure contract assets and contract liabilities in a business combination in accordance with Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) Topic 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers (Topic 606). This guidance will be effective for us in the first quarter of 2023 on a prospective basis, with early adoption permitted. An accounting policy is deemed to be critical if it requires an accounting estimate to be made based on assumptions about matters that are highly uncertain at the time the estimate is made, if different estimates reasonably could have been used, or if changes in the estimate that are reasonably possible could materially impact the financial statements. We believe that the assumptions and estimates associated with revenue recognition for payments and other fees, income taxes, share-based compensation, loss contingencies, and business combinations and valuation of goodwill and other acquired intangible assets have the greatest potential impact on our consolidated financial statements. Therefore, we consider these to be our critical accounting policies and estimates. For further information on all of our significant accounting policies, see Note 1 of our accompanying Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements included in Part II, Item 8, "Financial Statements and Supplementary Data" of this Annual Report on Form 10-K.

We allocate the fair value of purchase consideration to the tangible assets acquired, liabilities assumed and intangible assets acquired based on their estimated fair values. The excess of the fair value of purchase consideration over the fair values of these identifiable assets and liabilities is recorded as goodwill. question: How did Meta Platforms, Inc.'s description of valuation techniques for financial instruments in its fiscal year 2018 10-K differ from its fiscal year 2015 10-K regarding the specific instruments mentioned?
ground_truth_answer: In fiscal year 2018, Meta described its valuation techniques for money market funds and marketable debt securities as being derived from quoted market prices or alternative pricing sources and models utilizing market observable inputs, but did not mention contingent consideration. In contrast, the fiscal year 2015 filing additionally described the valuation technique for contingent consideration liability as being based on the present value of probability-weighted future cash flows related to the contingent earn-out criteria and the fair value of common stock.
target_sections: Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
answer:
In fiscal year 2015, Meta stated that its valuation techniques used to measure the fair value of money market funds and marketable debt securities were derived from quoted market prices or alternative pricing sources and models utilizing market observable inputs, and it also stated that its valuation technique for the contingent consideration liability was based on the present value of probability-weighted future cash flows related to the contingent earn-out criteria and the fair value of its common stock on each reporting date [META FY2015, Item 8, META_FY2015_2015-12-31:313].  

In fiscal year 2018, Meta stated that its valuation techniques used to measure the fair value of money market funds and marketable debt securities were derived from quoted market prices or alternative pricing sources and models utilizing market observable inputs [META FY2018, Item 8, META_FY2018_2018-12-31:330].  

The difference is that the 2015 10-K specifically also described a valuation technique for the contingent consideration liability, while the 2018 10-K description mentioned only money market funds and marketable debt securities and did not include the contingent consideration liability [META FY2015, Item 8, META_FY2015_2015-12-31:313] [META FY2018, Item 8, META_FY2018_2018-12-31:330].

ground_truth_answer: 102.61%. Amazon said the increase in operating cash flow in 2017 was primarily due to the increase in net income, excluding non-cash charges such as depreciation, amortization, and stock-based compensation.

Amazon’s **cost or amortized cost of corporate debt securities** increased from **$2,105 million in 2016** to **$4,265 million in 2017** [6][7].

\]

Percentage decrease:

\[
\frac{41{,}304 - 39{,}440}{41{,}304} \times 100 \approx 4.5\%
\]

So, Apple’s total property, plant and equipment, net **decreased by approximately 4.5%** between fiscal 2018 and fiscal 2021 [2][1].

Net sales rose 28% or $50.9 billion during 2015 compared to 2014, driven by a 52% year-over-year increase in iPhone® net sales. iPhone net sales and unit sales in 2015 increased in all of the Company’s reportable operating segments. The Company also experienced year-over-year net sales increases in Mac®, Services and Other Products. Apple Watch®, which launched during the third quarter of 2015, accounted for more than 100% of the year-over-year growth in net sales of Other Products. Net sales growth during 2015 was partially offset by the effect of weakness in most foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar and lower iPad® net sales. The increase in net sales of Services during 2015 compared to 2014 was primarily due to growth from Internet Services and licensing. The increase in net sales of Services in 2014 compared to 2013 was primarily due to growth in net sales from Internet Services, AppleCare and licensing. Internet Services generated a total of $10.2 billion in net sales during 2014 compared to $9.3 billion during 2013. Growth in net sales from Internet Services was driven by increases in revenue from app sales reflecting continued growth in the installed base of iOS devices and the expanded offerings of iOS apps and related in-app purchases. This was partially offset by a decline in sales of digital music.

The year-over-year growth in iPhone net sales and unit sales during 2015 primarily resulted from strong demand for iPhone 6 and 6 Plus during 2015. question: Comparing Amazon.com Inc and JPMorgan Chase & Co in their fiscal year 2015 10-K filings, how do the primary competitive factors they cite for their respective retail and financial services businesses differ?
ground_truth_answer: In fiscal year 2015, Amazon cited selection, price, and convenience (specifically fast and reliable fulfillment) as the principal competitive factors for its retail businesses, while also noting service quality and reliability for its enterprise services. In contrast, JPMorgan Chase stated that its businesses generally compete on the basis of the quality and variety of products and services, transaction execution, innovation, reputation, and price, with competition varying by client type, industry, and geography.
target_sections: Item 1. Business
ITEM 1: BUSINESS
answer:
Amazon.com states that in its retail businesses, the principal competitive factors include selection, price, and convenience, including fast and reliable fulfillment. [AMZN FY2015, Item 1, AMZN_FY2015_2015-12-31:25]  

Amazon also says additional competitive factors for its seller and enterprise services include the quality, speed, and reliability of its services and tools, as well as customers’ ability and willingness to change business practices. [AMZN FY2015, Item 1, AMZN_FY2015_2015-12-31:25]  

More broadly, Amazon describes competition as coming from a wide range of sectors including retailers, publishers, logistics providers, IT and cloud services companies, e-commerce service providers, search and discovery platforms, and consumer device companies. [AMZN FY2015, Item 1, AMZN_FY2015_2015-12-31:24]  

Amazon further emphasizes that competitors may have greater resources, stronger brands, better supplier terms, more aggressive pricing, restrictive distribution arrangements, and greater ability to invest in technology, infrastructure, fulfillment, and marketing. [AMZN FY2015, Item 1, AMZN_FY2015_2015-12-31:25] [AMZN FY2015, Item 1A, AMZN_FY2015_2015-12-31:36]  

For JPMorgan Chase, the provided evidence blocks identify its business segments and financial services lines such as Consumer & Business Banking, Commercial Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, and Asset Management, but they do not disclose the primary competitive factors those businesses cite in the filing. [JPM FY2015, 10-K, JPM_FY2015_2015-12-31:8] [JPM FY2015, Item 15, JPM_FY2015_2015-12-31:280] [JPM FY2015, Item 15, JPM_FY2015_2015-12-31:302] [JPM FY2015, Item 15, JPM_FY2015_2015-12-31:377]  

So, based on the evidence provided, Amazon explicitly frames competition around customer-facing retail factors such as selection, price, convenience, and fulfillment quality, while JPMorgan’s specific cited competitive factors for its financial services businesses are not disclosed in the provided excerpts. question: How do Alphabet and Meta Platforms differ in their stated strategies for managing foreign currency exchange risk in their 2023 10-K filings, specifically regarding the use of derivative instruments?
ground_truth_answer: Alphabet actively uses derivative instruments, including foreign currency forward and option contracts (such as collars), to hedge foreign currency risk on assets, liabilities, and forecasted earnings. In contrast, Meta Platforms stated that as of its 2023 filing, it had not entered into derivatives or other financial instruments to hedge its foreign currency exchange risk, though it acknowledged it might do so in the future.
target_sections: ITEM 7A.QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK
Item 7A.Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
answer:
Alphabet states that it uses derivative instruments to manage risks relating to its ongoing business operations, with foreign exchange risk identified as the primary risk managed. [GOOGL FY2023, Item 8, GOOGL_FY2023_2023-12-31:373] Alphabet says it uses foreign currency contracts to reduce the risk that its cash flows, earnings, and investment in foreign subsidiaries will be adversely affected by foreign currency exchange rate fluctuations. [GOOGL FY2023, Item 8, GOOGL_FY2023_2023-12-31:373] Alphabet also states that it enters into foreign currency forward and option contracts to hedge foreign currency risk, and that principal currencies hedged included the Australian dollar, British pound, Canadian dollar, Euro, and Japanese yen. [GOOGL FY2023, Item 7A, GOOGL_FY2023_2023-12-31:255] Alphabet further says it uses foreign currency forward and option contracts, including collars, to protect forecasted U.S. dollar-equivalent earnings from changes in foreign currency exchange rates, designates these contracts as cash flow hedges for accounting purposes, and uses foreign exchange forward contracts designated as net investment hedges to hedge foreign currency risks related to investments in foreign subsidiaries. [GOOGL FY2023, Item 7A, GOOGL_FY2023_2023-12-31:257] [GOOGL FY2023, Item 7A, GOOGL_FY2023_2023-12-31:258] Alphabet also uses foreign currency forward and option contracts that are not designated as hedging instruments to hedge intercompany transactions and other monetary assets or liabilities denominated in currencies other than the functional currency of a subsidiary. [GOOGL FY2023, Item 8, GOOGL_FY2023_2023-12-31:377]

Meta states that it is exposed to foreign currency exchange risk related to revenue and operating expenses denominated in currencies other than the U.S. dollar, primarily the Euro. [META FY2023, Item 7A, META_FY2023_2023-12-31:401] However, Meta says that, at this time, it has not entered into derivatives or other financial instruments to hedge its foreign currency exchange risk, although it may do so in the future. [META FY2023, Item 7A, META_FY2023_2023-12-31:402] Meta therefore describes foreign currency transaction gains or losses from remeasuring monetary asset and liability balances, rather than an active derivative hedging program. [META FY2023, Item 7A, META_FY2023_2023-12-31:402]

In short, Alphabet describes an active and multi-faceted derivative hedging strategy for foreign currency risk, including cash flow hedges, net investment hedges, and non-designated derivatives, while Meta says it had not entered into derivatives or other financial instruments to hedge foreign currency exchange risk as of its 2023 filing. ITEM 8.FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND SUPPLEMENTARY DATA > Derivative Financial Instruments
We use derivative instruments to manage risks relating to our ongoing business operations. The primary risk managed is foreign exchange risk. We use foreign currency contracts to reduce the risk that our cash flows, earnings, and investment in foreign subsidiaries will be adversely affected by foreign currency exchange rate fluctuations. We also enter into derivative instruments to partially offset our exposure to other risks and enhance investment returns. We recognize derivative instruments in the Consolidated Balance Sheets at fair value and classify the derivatives primarily within Level 2 in the fair value hierarchy. We present our collar contracts (an option strategy comprised of a combination of purchased and written options) at net fair values and present all other derivatives at gross fair values. The accounting treatment for derivatives is based on the intended use and hedge designation.

ITEM 7A.QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK > Foreign Currency Exchange Risk
We transact business globally in multiple currencies. International revenues, as well as costs and expenses denominated in foreign currencies, expose us to the risk of fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates against the U.S. dollar. As discussed below, we enter into derivative instruments to hedge foreign currency risk. Principal currencies hedged included the Australian dollar, British pound, Canadian dollar, Euro, and Japanese yen. For the purpose of analyzing foreign currency exchange risk, we considered the historical trends in foreign currency exchange rates and determined that it was reasonably possible that adverse changes in exchange rates of 10% could be experienced. We use foreign currency forward and option contracts to offset the foreign exchange risk on assets and liabilities denominated in currencies other than the functional currency of the subsidiary. These forward and option contracts reduce, but do not entirely eliminate, the effect of foreign currency exchange rate movements on our assets and liabilities. The foreign currency gains and losses on these assets and liabilities are recorded in OI&E, which are offset by the gains and losses on the forward and option contracts.

ITEM 8.FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND SUPPLEMENTARY DATA > Other Derivatives
We enter into foreign currency forward and option contracts that are not designated as hedging instruments to hedge intercompany transactions and other monetary assets or liabilities denominated in currencies other than the functional currency of a subsidiary. Gains and losses on these derivatives that are not designated as accounting hedges are primarily recorded in OI&E along with the foreign currency gains and losses on monetary assets and liabilities. We also use derivatives not designated as hedging instruments to manage risks relating to interest rates, commodity prices, credit exposures, and to enhance investment returns. From time to time, we enter into derivatives to hedge the market price risk on certain of our marketable equity securities. Gains and losses arising from other derivatives are primarily reflected within the “other” component of OI&E. See Note 7 for further details. 68. Table of Contents Alphabet Inc. The gross notional amounts of outstanding derivative instruments were as follows (in millions):

ITEM 7A.QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK > Foreign Currency Exchange Risk
If an adverse 10% foreign currency exchange rate change was applied to total monetary assets, liabilities, and commitments denominated in currencies other than the functional currencies at the balance sheet date, it would have resulted in an adverse effect on income before income taxes of approximately $136 million and $503 million as of December 31, 2022 and 2023, respectively, after consideration of the effect of foreign exchange contracts in place for the years ended December 31, 2022 and 2023.

ITEM 7A.QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK > Foreign Currency Exchange Risk
If the U.S. dollar weakened by 10% as of December 31, 2022 and 2023, the amount recorded in AOCI related to our cash flow hedges before tax effect would have been approximately $1.3 billion and $1.5 billion lower as of December 31, 2022 and 2023, respectively. The change in the value recorded in AOCI would be expected to offset a corresponding foreign currency change in forecasted hedged revenues when recognized. We use foreign exchange forward contracts designated as net investment hedges to hedge the foreign currency risks related to investment in foreign subsidiaries. These forward contracts serve to offset the foreign currency translation risk from our foreign operations. If the U.S. dollar weakened by 10%, the amount recorded in cumulative translation adjustment (CTA) within AOCI related to our net investment hedges before tax effect would have been approximately $903 million and $946 million lower as of December 31, 2022 and 2023, respectively. The change in value recorded in CTA would be expected to offset a corresponding foreign currency translation gain or loss from our investment in foreign subsidiaries.

ITEM 7A.QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK > Foreign Currency Exchange Risk
We use foreign currency forward and option contracts, including collars (an option strategy comprised of a combination of purchased and written options) to protect forecasted U.S. dollar-equivalent earnings from changes in foreign currency exchange rates. When the U.S. dollar strengthens, gains from foreign currency forward and option contacts reduce the foreign currency losses related to our earnings. When the U.S. dollar weakens, losses from foreign currency forward and option contracts offset the foreign currency gains related to our earnings. These hedging contracts reduce, but do not entirely eliminate, the effect of foreign currency exchange rate movements. We designate these contracts as cash flow hedges for accounting purposes. We reflect the gains or losses of foreign currency spot rate changes as a component of accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) and subsequently reclassify them into revenues to offset the hedged exposures as they occur.

We have experienced and will continue to experience fluctuations in our net income as a result of transaction gains or losses related to remeasuring monetary asset and liability balances that are denominated in currencies other than the functional currency of the entities in which they are recorded. At this time, we have not entered into, but in the future we may enter into, derivatives or other financial instruments in an attempt to hedge our foreign currency exchange risk. It is difficult to predict the effect hedging activities would have on our results of operations. question: How did Meta Platforms, Inc. expand the scope of its risk disclosures regarding privacy, safety, and content review efforts between its 2018 and 2021 fiscal year 10-K filings, specifically reflecting changes in its operational practices and external oversight mechanisms?
ground_truth_answer: In its 2018 10-K, Meta disclosed costs related to its "safety, security, and content review efforts" without specific mention of voluntary practice changes or external oversight bodies. By the 2021 10-K, the company expanded this disclosure to include costs related to "privacy, safety, security, and content review efforts" and explicitly cited "implementing changes to our practices, whether voluntarily, in connection with laws, regulations, regulatory actions, or decisions or recommendations from the independent Oversight Board." This indicates a shift from general operational costs to a more detailed recognition of regulatory and independent governance influences on its cost structure.
target_sections: Item 1A.Risk Factors
Item 1A. Risk Factors
answer:
In its 2018 Form 10-K, Meta disclosed that it was making significant investments in safety, security, and content review efforts to combat misuse of its services and user data by third parties, including investigations and audits of platform applications that previously accessed information of a large number of users of its services. [META FY2018, Item 1A, META_FY2018_2018-12-31:74]

The 2018 disclosure focused on the possibility that these efforts would uncover additional incidents of misuse of user data or other undesirable third-party activity, including false or undesirable user accounts, election interference, improper ad purchases, threats to people’s safety, and spamming, scraping, or spreading misinformation. [META FY2018, Item 1A, META_FY2018_2018-12-31:74]

By 2021, Meta expanded this disclosure by stating that it was making significant investments not only in privacy, safety, security, and content review efforts, but also in enforcement efforts, and that these efforts included investigations and audits of platform applications as well as other enforcement efforts. [META FY2021, Item 1A, META_FY2021_2021-12-31:206]

The 2021 filing also broadened the operational limitations it identified, stating that Meta may not discover all such incidents because of data or technical limitations, lack of visibility over encrypted services, the scale of activity on its platform, challenges related to personnel working remotely during the COVID-19 pandemic, the allocation of resources to other projects, or other factors. [META FY2021, Item 1A, META_FY2021_2021-12-31:206]

Meta further expanded the external oversight dimension in 2021 by disclosing that it may be notified of incidents or activity by the independent privacy assessor required under its modified consent order with the FTC, in addition to the media or other third parties. [META FY2021, Item 1A, META_FY2021_2021-12-31:206]

The 2021 filing also described a much more formalized compliance and oversight structure tied to external regulation, stating that it was engaged in ongoing privacy compliance and oversight efforts in connection with its modified consent order with the FTC, the GDPR, the CCPA, and the ePrivacy Directive. [META FY2021, Item 1A, META_FY2021_2021-12-31:187]

Meta said that, in connection with the FTC consent order, it was maintaining a comprehensive privacy program that included substantial management and board of directors oversight, stringent operational requirements and reporting obligations, prohibitions against making misrepresentations relating to user data, a process to regularly certify compliance to the FTC, and regular assessments of its privacy program by an independent third-party assessor. [META FY2021, Item 1A, META_FY2021_2021-12-31:187]

The company also disclosed in 2021 that these compliance and oversight efforts were increasing demand on its systems and resources, requiring significant new and ongoing investments in compliance processes, personnel, and technical infrastructure, and causing internal resource reallocation that had adversely affected and would continue to adversely affect other business initiatives. [META FY2021, Item 1A, META_FY2021_2021-12-31:187]

In addition, Meta stated that these efforts required substantial modifications to its business practices and made some practices such as product and ads development more difficult, time-consuming, and costly, and that its ability to develop and launch new features, products, and services in a timely manner had been and would continue to be adversely affected. [META FY2021, Item 1A, META_FY2021_2021-12-31:187] [META FY2021, Item 1A, META_FY2021_2021-12-31:188]

The 2021 filing also added that Meta expected its privacy compliance and oversight efforts to require significant time and attention from management and the board of directors, and that failures to comply with the FTC consent order or other privacy requirements could lead to regulatory or governmental investigations or lawsuits and significant monetary penalties. [META FY2021, Item 1A, META_FY2021_2021-12-31:188]

Meta’s 2021 risk disclosures therefore expanded from a 2018 emphasis on internal investments to detect misuse and harmful activity into a broader framework that explicitly incorporated privacy-focused operational changes, formal compliance infrastructure, board-level governance, independent third-party assessment, and ongoing oversight by regulators under the FTC consent order and other privacy regimes. Item 1.Business > Government Regulation
We are subject to a variety of laws and regulations in the United States and abroad that involve matters central to our business, many of which are still evolving and being tested in courts, and could be interpreted in ways that could harm our business. These laws and regulations involve matters including privacy, data use, data protection and personal information, biometrics, encryption, rights of publicity, content, intellectual property, advertising, marketing, distribution, data security, data retention and deletion, data localization and storage, data disclosure, artificial intelligence, electronic contracts and other communications, competition, protection of minors, consumer protection, civil rights, telecommunications, product liability, e-commerce, taxation, economic or other trade controls including sanctions, anti-corruption and political law compliance, securities law compliance, and online payment services. In particular, we are subject to federal, state, and foreign laws regarding privacy and protection of people's data. Foreign data protection, privacy, content, competition, consumer protection, and other laws and regulations can impose different obligations, or penalties or fines for non-compliance, or be more restrictive than those in the United States.

question: How do the income tax discussions in Microsoft's and Alphabet's fiscal year 2019 MD&A differ in the U.S. tax law change or tax authority they highlight?
ground_truth_answer: Microsoft's 2019 10-K explicitly identifies the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) as a significant change to U.S. tax law that affects its business, while Alphabet's 2019 10-K focuses on the continuous examination of its returns by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and other tax authorities as the primary regulatory risk factor, without citing the TCJA.
target_sections: Item 7
ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS
answer:
Microsoft’s FY2019 MD&A highlights the **Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA)**, noting that it significantly changed U.S. tax law and affected Microsoft’s business, including provisional charges, an additional tax expense adjustment, and a later tax benefit tied to restructuring intangible property ownership [3][4].

Alphabet’s FY2019 income tax discussion highlights the **Tax Act enacted on December 22, 2017**, emphasizing that it **reduced the U.S. statutory tax rate from 35% to 21%** and created **new taxes on certain foreign-sourced earnings and related-party payments**, along with transition tax and deferred tax effects [1][5].

ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Walmart International Segment
Net sales for the Walmart International segment increased $7.2 billion or 6.3% and $13.7 billion or 13.5% for fiscal 2025 and 2024, respectively, when compared to the previous fiscal year. For fiscal 2025, the increase was primarily due to positive comparable sales in all of our international markets, which included strength in eCommerce, partially offset by negative fluctuations in currency exchange rates of $3.2 billion. For fiscal 2024, the increase was primarily due to positive comparable sales across our international markets and positive fluctuations in currency exchange rates of $3.0 billion. Gross profit rate increased 20 basis points for both fiscal 2025 and 2024 when compared to the previous fiscal year. For fiscal 2025, the increase was primarily due to improved eCommerce margin and business mix changes, partially offset by ongoing channel and format mix changes. For fiscal 2024, the increase was primarily driven by supply chain efficiencies partially offset by ongoing channel and format mix shifts.

ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Margin
(1) Gross profit defined as net sales less cost of sales. Gross profit as a percentage of net sales ("gross profit rate") increased 40 and 27 basis points for fiscal 2025 and 2024, respectively, when compared to the previous fiscal year. The increases were primarily driven by the Walmart U.S. segment, due to managing prices aligned to our competitive historic price gaps, as well as growth in higher margin businesses globally, partially offset by mix shifts into lower margin merchandise categories. Additionally, the increase in fiscal 2024 benefited from lapping higher markdowns incurred in the prior year. Operating expenses as a percentage of net sales increased 36 and decreased 60 basis points for fiscal 2025 and 2024, respectively, when compared to the previous fiscal year. The increase for fiscal 2025 was primarily due to higher variable pay as a result of exceeding planned performance, increased marketing and higher depreciation expenses. The decrease for fiscal 2024 was primarily due to lapping charges of $3.3 billion related to opioid-related legal settlements and $0.8 billion related to the reorganization and restructuring of certain businesses in the Walmart International segment in the prior year.

ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Walmart U.S. Segment
Gross profit rate increased 47 and 20 basis points for fiscal 2025 and 2024, respectively, when compared to the previous fiscal year. The increase in fiscal 2025 gross profit rate was primarily driven by managing prices aligned to our competitive historic price gaps and growth in higher margin businesses, partially offset by mix shifts into lower margin merchandise categories. The increase in fiscal 2024 gross profit rate was primarily due to managing prices aligned to our competitive historic price gaps and lapping higher net markdowns incurred in the prior year, partially offset by product mix shifts into lower margin categories. Operating expenses as a percentage of segment net sales increased 44 and 9 basis points for fiscal 2025 and 2024, respectively, when compared to the previous fiscal year. The increase for fiscal 2025 was primarily due to increased marketing expenses, higher variable pay as a result of exceeding planned performance and increased depreciation expenses. For fiscal 2024, the increase was driven by higher variable pay relative to the prior year as a result of exceeding our planned performance.

ground_truth_answer: $975 million. NVIDIA says its Tegra brand integrates an entire computer onto a single chip and incorporates GPUs and multi-core CPUs to drive supercomputing for autonomous robots, drones and cars, as well as for consoles and mobile gaming and entertainment devices.

question: How did Meta Platforms' accounting policy for recognizing credit losses on available-for-sale debt securities change between its fiscal year 2019 and fiscal year 2023 10-K filings?
ground_truth_answer: In its fiscal year 2019 10-K, Meta indicated that unrealized losses were charged against interest and other income, net, only when a decline in fair value was determined to be other-than-temporary, and noted that no such impairment charges had been recorded. In its fiscal year 2023 10-K, the policy evolved to align with newer accounting standards, where allowance for credit losses on AFS debt securities are recognized as a charge in interest and other income (expense), net, based on an assessment of expected credit losses, with any remaining unrealized losses included in accumulated other comprehensive income.
target_sections: Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
Item 8.Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
answer:
In Meta Platforms’ fiscal year 2019 10-K, unrealized losses on available-for-sale investments were charged against interest and other income, net when a decline in fair value was determined to be other-than-temporary, and the company stated it had not recorded any such impairment charge in the periods presented. [META FY2019, Item 8, META_FY2019_2019-12-31:365]

The fiscal year 2019 10-K also disclosed that ASU 2016-13 would be adopted effective January 1, 2020, replacing the existing incurred loss impairment model with a forward-looking expected credit loss model that requires the measurement and recognition of expected credit losses for financial assets held at amortized cost. [META FY2019, Item 8, META_FY2019_2019-12-31:390]

By Meta Platforms’ fiscal year 2023 10-K, available-for-sale debt securities with an amortized cost basis in excess of estimated fair value were assessed to determine what amount of that difference, if any, was caused by expected credit losses. [META FY2023, Item 8, META_FY2023_2023-12-31:464]

In the fiscal year 2023 10-K, allowance for credit losses on available-for-sale debt securities was recognized as a charge in interest and other income (expense), net on the consolidated statements of income, and any remaining unrealized losses, net of taxes, were included in accumulated other comprehensive income (loss) in stockholders’ equity. [META FY2023, Item 8, META_FY2023_2023-12-31:464]

So, the policy changed from an other-than-temporary impairment approach in 2019 to an expected credit loss approach with an allowance for credit losses on available-for-sale debt securities by 2023. question: How did JPMorgan Chase's 2023 10-K disclosure regarding the impact of market conditions on its wholesale businesses change in specificity compared to its 2018 disclosure, particularly regarding the types of capital markets activities explicitly identified as vulnerable to reduced profitability?
ground_truth_answer: The 2023 10-K provides a more specific enumeration of capital markets activities vulnerable to reduced profitability under adverse market conditions, explicitly listing 'loan syndication, securities underwriting and leveraged lending activities.' In contrast, the 2018 10-K referred more generally to 'capital markets businesses' and 'capital markets transactions' without explicitly listing leveraged lending in that specific context of reduced profitability, though it did mention loan syndications and securities underwritings in the context of transaction volumes and disposal losses.
target_sections: Item 1A. Risk Factors.
answer:
JPMorgan Chase’s 2023 disclosure remained similar to its 2018 disclosure in stating that unfavorable market and economic conditions can reduce transaction volumes and revenue in its wholesale businesses, and that a significant and sustained deterioration in market conditions could reduce profitability and fee revenue. [JPM FY2023, Item 1A, JPM_FY2023_2023-12-31:87] [JPM FY2018, Item 1A, JPM_FY2018_2018-12-31:77]

Compared with 2018, the 2023 filing was more specific in describing the affected businesses: in 2018 it referred to “JPMorgan Chase’s capital markets businesses,” while in 2023 it referred to “businesses engaged in capital markets activities, including loan syndication, securities underwriting and leveraged lending activities.” [JPM FY2023, Item 1A, JPM_FY2023_2023-12-31:87] [JPM FY2018, Item 1A, JPM_FY2018_2018-12-31:77]

The 2018 filing mentioned loan syndications and securities underwritings as examples of capital markets transactions JPMorgan Chase manages and as credit commitments that might be disposed of at a loss, but it did not explicitly include leveraged lending activities in that profitability sentence. [JPM FY2018, Item 1A, JPM_FY2018_2018-12-31:77]

So the added specificity in 2023 was the explicit identification of loan syndication, securities underwriting, and leveraged lending activities as capital markets activities whose profitability could be reduced by adverse market conditions. [JPM FY2023, Item 1A, JPM_FY2023_2023-12-31:87] [JPM FY2018, Item 1A, JPM_FY2018_2018-12-31:77]

If the U.S. dollar weakened by 10% as of December 31, 2019 and 2020, the amount recorded in AOCI related to our foreign exchange contracts before tax effect would have been approximately $1.1 billion and $912 million lower as of December 31, 2019 and 2020, respectively. The change in the value recorded in AOCI would be expected to offset a corresponding foreign currency change in forecasted hedged revenues when recognized. If the U.S. dollar weakened by 10%, the amount recorded in cumulative translation adjustment ("CTA") within AOCI related to our net investment hedge would have been approximately $936 million and $1 billion lower as of December 31, 2019 and 2020, respectively. ITEM 7A.QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK > Foreign Currency Exchange Risk
We use foreign currency forwards and option contracts, including collars (an option strategy comprised of a combination of purchased and written options) to protect our forecasted U.S. dollar-equivalent earnings from changes in foreign currency exchange rates. When the U.S. dollar strengthens, gains from foreign currency options and forwards reduce the foreign currency losses related to our earnings. When the U.S. dollar weakens, losses from foreign currency collars and forwards offset the foreign currency gains related to our earnings. These hedging contracts reduce, but do not entirely eliminate, the effect of foreign currency exchange rate movements. We designate these contracts as cash flow hedges for accounting purposes. We reflect the gains or losses of foreign currency spot rate changes as a component of AOCI and subsequently reclassify them into revenues to offset the hedged exposures as they occur.

Since R&D is a large component of operating expenses, this indicates operating expenses are less tightly correlated with current revenue than they would be if they moved directly with sales [1][10].

target_sections: Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
answer:
Apple’s weighted-average commercial paper interest rate decreased from 5.28% in 2023 to 5.00% in 2024 [1].

Year-over-year percentage change:

\[
\frac{5.00\% - 5.28\%}{5.28\%} \times 100 \approx -5.3\%
\]

So, the weighted-average interest rate **decreased by approximately 5.3% year over year** [1].

question: By how many percentage points did the dilutive effect of Amazon's outstanding stock awards, measured as a percentage of the shares used to compute basic earnings per share, change from fiscal year 2018 to fiscal year 2024?
ground_truth_answer: -0.30 percentage points (from about 2.67% in 2018 to about 2.37% in 2024)
target_sections: Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
answer:
In 2018, the dilutive effect as a percentage of basic shares was:

- 13 / 487 = about 2.67% [2]

In 2024, the dilutive effect as a percentage of basic shares was:

- 248 / 10,473 = about 2.37% [1]

Change from 2018 to 2024:

- 2.37% − 2.67% = about **-0.30 percentage points**

So, the dilutive effect **decreased by about 0.30 percentage points** from fiscal year 2018 to fiscal year 2024. [1][2]

question: How did the primary drivers for iPhone and Wearables, Home and Accessories net sales change for Apple Inc. between fiscal year 2020 and fiscal year 2025?
ground_truth_answer: In fiscal year 2020, iPhone net sales decreased primarily due to the absence of new iPhone models in the fourth quarter and foreign currency weakness, while Wearables, Home and Accessories net sales increased due to higher sales of AirPods and Apple Watch. By fiscal year 2025, iPhone net sales increased due to higher net sales of Pro models, whereas Wearables, Home and Accessories net sales decreased primarily due to lower net sales of Accessories and Wearables.
target_sections: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
answer:
Between fiscal year 2020 and fiscal year 2025, the primary drivers changed as follows:

- **iPhone**
  - In **2020**, iPhone net sales **decreased** primarily due to the **absence of new iPhone models in the fourth quarter of 2020** and **weakness in foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar**, partially offset by the **introduction of iPhone SE in the third quarter of 2020** [1].
  - In **2025**, iPhone net sales **increased** due to **higher net sales of Pro models** [4].

- **Wearables, Home and Accessories**
  - In **2020**, net sales **increased** primarily due to **higher net sales of AirPods and Apple Watch** [2].
  - In **2025**, net sales **decreased** primarily due to **lower net sales of Accessories and Wearables** [4].

So, overall, Apple went from:
- **iPhone** being pressured in 2020 by timing of product launches and currency weakness to being driven upward in 2025 by strong **Pro model** sales [1][4].
- **Wearables, Home and Accessories** being driven upward in 2020 by **AirPods and Apple Watch** to declining in 2025 because of weaker **Accessories and Wearables** sales [2][4].

question: How do Alphabet and Meta Platforms differ in their stated strategies for managing foreign currency exchange risk in their 2023 10-K filings, specifically regarding the use of derivative instruments?
ground_truth_answer: Alphabet actively uses derivative instruments, including foreign currency forward and option contracts (such as collars), to hedge foreign currency risk on assets, liabilities, and forecasted earnings. In contrast, Meta Platforms stated that as of its 2023 filing, it had not entered into derivatives or other financial instruments to hedge its foreign currency exchange risk, though it acknowledged it might do so in the future.
target_sections: ITEM 7A.QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK
Item 7A.Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
answer:
Alphabet states that it uses derivative instruments to manage foreign exchange risk, including foreign currency forward and option contracts to offset foreign exchange risk on assets and liabilities denominated in currencies other than a subsidiary’s functional currency, and it identifies principal currencies hedged as the Australian dollar, British pound, Canadian dollar, Euro, and Japanese yen [GOOGL FY2023, Item 8, GOOGL_FY2023_2023-12-31:373] [GOOGL FY2023, Item 7A, GOOGL_FY2023_2023-12-31:255].  

Alphabet also states that it uses foreign currency forward and option contracts, including collars, to protect forecasted U.S. dollar-equivalent earnings from changes in foreign currency exchange rates, designates these contracts as cash flow hedges for accounting purposes, and records spot-rate gains or losses in AOCI before reclassifying them into revenues as the hedged exposures occur [GOOGL FY2023, Item 7A, GOOGL_FY2023_2023-12-31:257].  

In addition, Alphabet says it enters into foreign currency forward and option contracts that are not designated as hedging instruments to hedge intercompany transactions and other monetary assets or liabilities denominated in currencies other than the functional currency of a subsidiary, with gains and losses primarily recorded in OI&E [GOOGL FY2023, Item 8, GOOGL_FY2023_2023-12-31:377].  

By contrast, Meta states that it has not entered into derivatives or other financial instruments to hedge its foreign currency exchange risk, although it may do so in the future [META FY2023, Item 7A, META_FY2023_2023-12-31:402].  

So, Alphabet’s 2023 filing describes an active derivative-based foreign currency risk management program using forwards, options, and collars, including both designated cash flow hedges and non-designated hedges, while Meta’s 2023 filing says it was not using derivatives for foreign currency hedging at that time [GOOGL FY2023, Item 8, GOOGL_FY2023_2023-12-31:373] [GOOGL FY2023, Item 8, GOOGL_FY2023_2023-12-31:377] [GOOGL FY2023, Item 7A, GOOGL_FY2023_2023-12-31:257] [META FY2023, Item 7A, META_FY2023_2023-12-31:402].

ITEM 8.FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND SUPPLEMENTARY DATA > Derivative Financial Instruments
We use derivative instruments to manage risks relating to our ongoing business operations. The primary risk managed is foreign exchange risk. We use foreign currency contracts to reduce the risk that our cash flows, earnings, and investment in foreign subsidiaries will be adversely affected by foreign currency exchange rate fluctuations. We also enter into derivative instruments to partially offset our exposure to other risks and enhance investment returns. We recognize derivative instruments in the Consolidated Balance Sheets at fair value and classify the derivatives primarily within Level 2 in the fair value hierarchy. We present our collar contracts (an option strategy comprised of a combination of purchased and written options) at net fair values and present all other derivatives at gross fair values. The accounting treatment for derivatives is based on the intended use and hedge designation.

ITEM 7A.QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK > Foreign Currency Exchange Risk
We transact business globally in multiple currencies. International revenues, as well as costs and expenses denominated in foreign currencies, expose us to the risk of fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates against the U.S. dollar. As discussed below, we enter into derivative instruments to hedge foreign currency risk. Principal currencies hedged included the Australian dollar, British pound, Canadian dollar, Euro, and Japanese yen. For the purpose of analyzing foreign currency exchange risk, we considered the historical trends in foreign currency exchange rates and determined that it was reasonably possible that adverse changes in exchange rates of 10% could be experienced. We use foreign currency forward and option contracts to offset the foreign exchange risk on assets and liabilities denominated in currencies other than the functional currency of the subsidiary. These forward and option contracts reduce, but do not entirely eliminate, the effect of foreign currency exchange rate movements on our assets and liabilities. The foreign currency gains and losses on these assets and liabilities are recorded in OI&E, which are offset by the gains and losses on the forward and option contracts.

ITEM 8.FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND SUPPLEMENTARY DATA > Other Derivatives
We enter into foreign currency forward and option contracts that are not designated as hedging instruments to hedge intercompany transactions and other monetary assets or liabilities denominated in currencies other than the functional currency of a subsidiary. Gains and losses on these derivatives that are not designated as accounting hedges are primarily recorded in OI&E along with the foreign currency gains and losses on monetary assets and liabilities. We also use derivatives not designated as hedging instruments to manage risks relating to interest rates, commodity prices, credit exposures, and to enhance investment returns. From time to time, we enter into derivatives to hedge the market price risk on certain of our marketable equity securities. Gains and losses arising from other derivatives are primarily reflected within the “other” component of OI&E. See Note 7 for further details. 68. Table of Contents Alphabet Inc. The gross notional amounts of outstanding derivative instruments were as follows (in millions):

ITEM 7A.QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK > Foreign Currency Exchange Risk
We use foreign currency forward and option contracts, including collars (an option strategy comprised of a combination of purchased and written options) to protect forecasted U.S. dollar-equivalent earnings from changes in foreign currency exchange rates. When the U.S. dollar strengthens, gains from foreign currency forward and option contacts reduce the foreign currency losses related to our earnings. When the U.S. dollar weakens, losses from foreign currency forward and option contracts offset the foreign currency gains related to our earnings. These hedging contracts reduce, but do not entirely eliminate, the effect of foreign currency exchange rate movements. We designate these contracts as cash flow hedges for accounting purposes. We reflect the gains or losses of foreign currency spot rate changes as a component of accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) and subsequently reclassify them into revenues to offset the hedged exposures as they occur.

ITEM 7A.QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK > Foreign Currency Exchange Risk
If an adverse 10% foreign currency exchange rate change was applied to total monetary assets, liabilities, and commitments denominated in currencies other than the functional currencies at the balance sheet date, it would have resulted in an adverse effect on income before income taxes of approximately $136 million and $503 million as of December 31, 2022 and 2023, respectively, after consideration of the effect of foreign exchange contracts in place for the years ended December 31, 2022 and 2023.

Item 7A.Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk > Foreign Currency Exchange Risk
We have experienced and will continue to experience fluctuations in our net income as a result of transaction gains or losses related to remeasuring monetary asset and liability balances that are denominated in currencies other than the functional currency of the entities in which they are recorded. At this time, we have not entered into, but in the future we may enter into, derivatives or other financial instruments in an attempt to hedge our foreign currency exchange risk. It is difficult to predict the effect hedging activities would have on our results of operations. Foreign currency exchange net losses of $366 million, $81 million, and $140 million were recognized in 2023, 2022, and 2021, respectively.

question: How does Amazon's seasonal retail demand pattern affect its cash and accounts payable balances as of December 31?
ground_truth_answer: As of December 31, Amazon's cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities balances typically reach their highest level because consumers primarily use credit cards in its stores and the related receivables settle quickly. Correspondingly, there is typically an increase in accounts payable due to inventory purchases and third-party seller sales.
target_sections: Item 1A. Risk Factors
answer:
Amazon states that holiday sales typically cause its cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities balances to reach their highest level as of December 31 because consumers primarily use credit cards and the related receivables settle quickly. [AMZN FY2025, Item 1A, AMZN_FY2025_2025-12-31:48]

Amazon also states that there is typically a corresponding increase in accounts payable as of December 31 due to inventory purchases and third-party seller sales. [AMZN FY2025, Item 1A, AMZN_FY2025_2025-12-31:48]

The filing further says that during the first three months of the following year, accounts payable generally declines as vendors and sellers are paid, resulting in a corresponding decline in cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities balances. [AMZN FY2025, Item 1A, AMZN_FY2025_2025-12-31:48]

This seasonal pattern is consistent with Amazon’s operating model of collecting from consumers before payments to vendors and sellers become due. [AMZN FY2025, Item 7, AMZN_FY2025_2025-12-31:115]

Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations > Overview
We seek to turn inventory quickly and collect from consumers before our payments to vendors and sellers become due. Because consumers primarily use credit cards in our stores, our receivables from consumers settle quickly. We expect variability in inventory turnover over time since it is affected by numerous factors, including our product mix, the mix of sales by us and by third-party sellers, our continuing focus on in-stock inventory availability and selection of product offerings, supply chain disruptions and resulting vendor lead times, our investment in new geographies and product lines, and the extent to which we choose to utilize third-party fulfillment providers. We also expect some variability in accounts payable days over time since they are affected by several factors, including the mix of product sales, the mix of sales by third-party sellers, the mix of suppliers, seasonality, and changes in payment and other terms over time, including the effect of balancing pricing and timing of payment terms with suppliers.

ground_truth_answer: 40.93% decrease (from $623 million to $368 million). Meta lists valuation of long-lived assets, including goodwill, intangible assets and property and equipment and their estimated useful lives, among the assumptions and estimates with the greatest potential impact on its consolidated financial statements, so it treats them as critical accounting policies and estimates.

\]

question: Compare how Alphabet Inc. and Apple Inc. described their interest rate risk management strategies in their fiscal year 2023 10-K filings, specifically highlighting the difference between Alphabet's use of value-at-risk analysis and Apple's specific defensive instruments.
ground_truth_answer: In its fiscal year 2023 10-K, Alphabet described its interest rate risk management using a value-at-risk (VaR) analysis with a 95% confidence interval to determine the potential effect of interest rate fluctuations on its marketable debt security portfolio. In contrast, Apple's fiscal year 2023 10-K stated that to protect against interest rate risk, the company may use derivative instruments, offset interest rate-sensitive assets and liabilities, or control the duration of its investment and term debt portfolios.
target_sections: ITEM 7A.QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK
Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
answer:
Alphabet and Apple described interest rate risk differently in their FY2023 10-Ks:

- **Alphabet Inc.** said it **uses value-at-risk (VaR) analysis** to measure the potential effect of interest rate fluctuations on the value of its **marketable debt security portfolio**. It defined VaR as the expected loss in fair value for a given confidence interval and stated it uses a **variance/covariance VaR model with a 95% confidence interval**. This is primarily a **risk measurement/assessment approach**. [1]

- **Apple Inc.** said it is exposed to U.S. interest rate fluctuations affecting both its **investment portfolio and term debt**, and that to protect against this risk it may use **derivative instruments**, **offset interest rate-sensitive assets and liabilities**, or **control duration of the investment and term debt portfolios**. This is a more explicit description of **defensive risk management tools and actions**. [4]

So, the key difference is that **Alphabet emphasized VaR as an analytical method for quantifying interest rate risk**, while **Apple specifically identified instruments and portfolio management techniques it may use to mitigate that risk**, such as derivatives and duration control. [1][4]

The OBBBA introduces multiple tax law and other legislative changes, including modifications to income tax provisions such as domestic research and development expenses, capital expenditures, and U.S. taxation of international earnings; the repeal or acceleration of the sunset of certain tax credits under the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act and elimination of certain penalties for violations of certain regulatory credit programs. We have recognized the effects of the OBBBA provisions in our financial results to the extent they are applicable to the year ended December 31, 2025. We will continue to evaluate the impact of these provisions on our 2026 and subsequent consolidated financial statements, including loss of certain regulatory credit sales tied to our products and changes to the costs of our products.

ITEM 9B. OTHER INFORMATION
On January 16, 2026, following review in a manner consistent with the Board’s fiduciary duties and the Company’s related party transactions policy (the “RPT Policy”), Tesla entered into an agreement to invest approximately $2 billion to acquire shares of Series E Preferred Stock of xAI as part of xAI’s recent publicly-disclosed financing round. Tesla’s investment was made on market terms consistent with those already received by other investors in the financing, including with respect to price, customary information rights and registration rights. Completion of the investment is subject to customary limited closing conditions, including applicable regulatory approvals. As previously disclosed, Tesla and xAI have certain ongoing commercial relationships that are described in the Company’s proxy statement for its 2025 Annual Meeting of Shareholders (the “2025 Proxy Statement”). In connection with the investment, Tesla and xAI also entered into certain framework agreement that, among other things, builds upon the existing relationship between Tesla and xAI by providing a framework for evaluating potential collaborations, with any specific projects to be implemented through separate negotiations, all of which will be subject to applicable approval processes (including the RPT Policy) and in a manner consistent with the Board’s fiduciary duties.
